questions.question: Two normalised densities have difference $d=f_X-f_Y$, non-negative below a threshold and non-positive above it. Why can their CDF difference $D(t)=F_X(t)-F_Y(t)$ not become negative after that threshold?
options: The remaining tail satisfies $D(t)=-\int_t^\infty d(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\ge0$.
The density difference must remain non-negative there.
The CDF difference equals the pointwise value of d.
The later density values no longer affect either CDF.

questions.question: On $(0,1)$, losses have density versions $f_X(t)=2(1-t)$ and $f_Y(t)=2t$, both zero elsewhere. At what point does their difference change from positive to negative?
On $(0,1)$, $f_X(t)=2(1-t)$ and $f_Y(t)=2t$, zero elsewhere. What is $\mathbb{P}(X\le1/4)$, the lower-tail area used in their crossing comparison?
On $(0,1)$, $f_X(t)=2(1-t)$ and $f_Y(t)=2t$, with CDFs $F_X(t)=2t-t^2$ and $F_Y(t)=t^2$. At $t=3/4$, what are the signs of density difference and CDF difference?
options: Density gap negative; CDF gap positive.
Density gap negative; CDF gap negative.
Density gap positive; CDF gap positive.
Density gap positive; CDF gap negative.

questions.question: $X$ has density $1/2$ on $(0,2)$. $Y$ has density $3/4$ on $(0,1/2)\cup(3/2,2)$ and $1/4$ on $(1/2,3/2)$; both are zero elsewhere. Their densities are symmetric about 1. Which mean pair supports the two-crossing thicker-tail criterion?
options: X has mean 1; Y has mean 3/2.
X has mean 1; Y has mean 1/2.
Both means equal 2.
Both means equal 1.

questions.question: For two normalised equal-mean densities, $f_Y-f_X$ has signs positive, negative, positive on three regions. Does the CDF crossing have to occur at one of the two density crossings?
options: Yes; integrating leaves every crossing point fixed.
Yes; the first density crossing is always the CDF crossing.
Yes; the second density crossing is always the CDF crossing.
No; the cumulative gap depends on integrated signed areas.

questions.question: $X=1$ surely; $Y$ equals 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Both means are 1. Their CDF difference $F_Y-F_X$ is positive below 1 and negative at 1. Which crossing convention correctly describes this direct thicker-tail comparison?
options: Both sides include 1 and demand equality there.
Lower side t<1; upper side t≥1.
Lower side t≤1; upper side t>1.
Discard the point t=1 as a density-version choice.
